title: 1  Sets
text:
1.1 Sets
This chapter is meant to be a quick introduction to sets. It is placed here so that it may be easily referenced.
Sets are a collection objects where there is no ordering. Elements are not repeated or counted. Sets can contain any object, including other sets, or they can be empty. The empty set is denoted by \(\emptyset\) or \(\{\}\) and is sometimes called the null set. Typically we use curly brackets to denote set notation. Thus a set described in enumeration notation as \(\{a,b,c\}\) is a set that contains elements \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). The order of the elements does not matter. Thus \(\{a,b,c\}\) is the same set as \(\{b,c,a\}\) or \(\{b, a, c\}\). If \(d\) were added to this set, we would have a new set \(\{a,b,c,d\}\), which is different from the original set. If \(a\) were added to the original set, we would still have the same set \(\{a,b,c\}\) because \(a\) is already an element of the set. Thus, elements are not repeated or counted in sets.
We will use enumeration notation right away to start describing important elements for this book. Enumeration notation is most often used when all items in a set can be easily described, the set is finite, or when a pattern can be easily inferred. Since easily inferred is subjective, we find it best to be explicit in our descriptions and notations.
Occasionally, set notation is easier than describing a set in English. For example, “the set containing the set that contains a” can be written as \(\{\{a\}\}\), which is easier to read and understand than the English description. This is an example of a set that contains another set. The inner set \(\{a\}\) is an element of the outer set \(\{\{a\}\}\). The inner set \(\{a\}\) contains the element \(a\). Thus, \(a\) is an element of the inner set \(\{a\}\), and the inner set \(\{a\}\) is an element of the outer set \(\{\{a\}\}\).
As some sets are infinite, we need a way to describe them without enumerating all of their elements. Set-builder notation is a way to describe sets by stating the properties that its members must satisfy. For example, the set of all even integers can be described in set-builder notation as \(\{x \mid x \text{ is an even integer}\}\). This can be read as “the set of all \(x\) such that \(x\) is an even integer”. The vertical bar \(|\) can be read as “such that”. In programming we often think of this pipe as an “OR” symbol, but we must think of it differently when it is in set-builder notation. Another example is \(\{w \mid w\) is a list of letters with one letter containing an \(a\}\), which can be read as “the set of all \(w\) such that \(w\) is a list of letters and one of those letters is an \(a\)”. Think of this notation in two pieces. The first piece is the variable \(w\) that represents the elements of the set. The second piece is the condition that describes the properties of the elements of the set. In this case, the condition is that \(w\) is a list of letters and one of those letters is an \(a\). This is not unlike a variable assignment in programming. We are assigning the variable \(w\) to represent the elements of the set, and we are describing the properties of those elements with the condition.
A subset is a collection of the elements of a set. For example, if we have the set \(\{a,b,c\}\), then \(\{a,b\}\) is a subset of \(\{a,b,c\}\) because it contains only elements that are in \(\{a,b,c\}\). We can also say that \(\{a,b,c\}\) is a superset of \(\{a,b\}\) because it contains all the elements of \(\{a,b\}\). The empty set is a subset of every set because it does not contain any elements that are not in any other set. Thus, \(\emptyset\) is a subset of every set. We use the symbol \(\subseteq\) to denote subset and \(\supseteq\) to denote superset. Thus, we can write \(\{a,b\} \subseteq \{a,b,c\}\) and \(\{a,b,c\} \supseteq \{a,b\}\).
When we are new to sets, this new vocabulary and its usage can be overwhelming. It is important to practice using this vocabulary and notation to become comfortable with it. The more you practice, the more natural it will become. We will be using it throughout the book, and thus you will have plenty of opportunities to practice.
The power set of a set is the set of all subsets of that set. For example, the power set of \(\{a,b\}\) is \(\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\}\). The power set of a set with \(n\) elements has \(2^n\) elements. Thus, the power set of a set with 2 elements has \(2^2 = 4\) elements, which we can see in the example above. The power set of a set with 3 elements has \(2^3 = 8\) elements, and so on. The power set of a set is denoted by \(\mathcal{P}(S)\), where \(S\) is the original set. Thus, we can write \(\mathcal{P}(\{a,b\}) = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\}\).
The union of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all elements that are in \(A\) or in \(B\) (or in both). The union of \(A\) and \(B\) is denoted by \(A \cup B\). For example, if \(A = \{a,b\}\) and \(B = \{b,c\}\), then \(A \cup B = \{a,b,c\}\). Remember that sets do not care about order and duplication.
The intersection of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all elements that are in both \(A\) and \(B\). The intersection of \(A\) and \(B\) is denoted by \(A \cap B\). For example, if \(A = \{a,b\}\) and \(B = \{b,c\}\), then \(A \cap B = \{b\}\). It is not uncommon for the intersection of two sets to be the empty set. For example, the intersection of the set of positive integers and the set of negative integers is simply \(\emptyset\).
To get comfortable with these new terms and operators, we must use them. We will be using them throughout the book, and thus you will have plenty of opportunities to practice. The more you practice, the more natural it will become. Occasionally, these concepts will appear as we tackle the material in the following chapters. Most things we talk about in this class are sets, because sets help us talk about collections of objects.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.1 Alphabets, Strings, and Languages
This chapter discusses strategies for understanding and working with deterministic finite automata (DFAs). We will cover the basics of DFAs, including their definition, how to construct them, and how to use them to recognize languages. We will be using examples and exercises to help practice and solidify our understanding of DFAs. By the end of this chapter, we should have a good grasp of what DFAs are, how they work, and how to use them effectively.
To start thinking about theory of computation, we define a few useful terms. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. For example, the binary alphabet is \(\{0,1\}\). A string is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. A string is not a set and order matters. Some example strings, using the binary alphabet, are \(1011\) and \(0101\). These are not unlike a string defined with quotation marks in a programming language like C++. We might write "1011" in C++ to represent a string. "1011" is a string that contains 4 characters. In this book, we refer to the characters as symbols, although, at times, the symbols have meaning. '0' is a symbol, an element of an alphabet, but it may also mean the digit 0. In this book, the empty string is denoted by a tilde, ~. The empty string is a string that contains no symbols. We often use empty strings in programming as well. In C++, we might set a string equal to the empty string, denoted by "". A language is a set of strings. The alphabet of the language is the set of symbols that can be used to create the strings in the language. We might have a language that contains all strings of even length. This language contains strings such as "", 00, 11, 0101, and so on if we’re using a binary alphabet. The language of all strings of even length over the binary alphabet can be denoted as \(L = \{w \mid w\) is a binary string of even length\(\}\). This is an example of a language that contains an infinite number of strings. We will be working with languages that contain both finite and infinite numbers of strings. Test understanding of these definitions with the following exercises.
As we continue, we will use these terms, alphabet, string, and language, frequently. Our alphabets are finite sets that define the characters that are allowed in our strings. Our strings are like words; they are an ordered list of characters. Our languages are sets of strings and they will often be infinite sets (having an unbounded number of strings).

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.2 Finite Automata (FA)
Finite automata (FA) are a type of computational model. In this text we will use the word machine synonymously with automata. Automata utilize states as a kind of finite memory. We might say that a FA can be used to determine if an input string is in the language of the machine. We will use some words interchangably at first and then expand their definitions. A machine recognizes a language but many machines may recognize the same language. States are represented using circles and machines are made up of states with transitions between them. In our diagrams, a state with a straight arrow pointing at it (not from another state) is the start state. A state with a double circle is an accept state. When a machine (specifically a DFA) processes a string, it will end in some state. If that state is an accept state, the machine accepts the string. If it is not, the machine rejects the string. The set of strings a machine accepts is the language of the machine. In the next chapter we’ll introduce more pieces for FAs to move things in line with how we think as programmers. But it is useful to understand this traditional model first.
Let’s explore the idea of FA with some real world examples. In figure Figure 2.1, we explore a sample state machine that we often see. Let’s take a look before we dive in.











Figure 2.1: Red-Yellow-Green - The Stoplight State Machine



In figure Figure 2.1, we see three states represented by circles: Red (RED), Green (GRN), and Yellow (YEL). There are no accept states. The arrows describe how we can transition from one state to the next. For example, to transition from Yellow to Red, we must see the end of a timer - denoted by t in the diagram. To go from Red to Green, a certain timer must trigger, but also, someone must be waiting at the sensor - denoted by s. This is a state machine for a side street. The side street never turns green unless someone is waiting at the sensor. Lastly, we turn the stoplight yellow after some time has passed and there is no longer someone waiting at the sensor. You might imagine slightly more complex logic on this transition, but to get us started, this is sufficient. Putting it all together, we have the state machine of a stop light. There are no accept states here and so the language being recognized by the machine is empty, but you can see the basics of how state machines are all around us from signals to controllers of other basic machinery.
Let’s examine a traditional deterministic finite automata that fits within the concepts of our work in theory of computation. Examine Figure 2.2 for a moment before we discuss it. Maybe we can decipher it’s language already!











Figure 2.2: A simple deterministic finite automata (DFA)



Could we figure out it’s language? Let’s take a look at Figure 2.2 a second time. What are some things that we notice? Well, when we see an input of 1, we stay in the same state. This means that an input of 1 will not move us around the states. We stay put when we eat an input of 1. On the other hand, an input of 0 does force us to change states. So, one 0 takes us away but another 0 brings us back. Lastly, we note that B is our accept state. To get there we need to see a 0. To stay there we need to see an even number of 0s. So, ignoring 1s, we end up in B after an odd number of 0s (an even number plus 1 to get us there to start with). This tells us ALL the strings that are recognized by this machine. Remember that the set of strings recognized by a machine is the language of the machine. In this case the language is all strings that have an odd number of 0s. Let’s practice with our set notation and play with this FA in the next exercises.






NoteDeterministic Finite Automata Exercise




Name a few real world situations that likely are driven by state machines.
Write the language in the machine of Figure 2.2 in set-builder notation.
If we mark A as an accept state and remove B as an accept state in Figure 2.2, what is the new language of the machine?
Make a machine that can accept any string with an even number of 1s.
Make a machine that can accept any string with \(3n\) number of 0s where \(n \geq 0\). The number of 1s does not matter.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.3 Frequently Used Language Elements
Now that we have a basic understanding of DFAs, it’ll be useful to take a look at some commonly used features of DFAs. Let’s start with strings that begin with a sequence. Perhaps you’re looking at a language defined as \(\{w \mid w\) begins with \(01\}\). To build this DFA, we’ll need four states. A start state, a state where we have “seen a 0”, a state where we have “seen 0 followed by 1”. The “seen 0 followed by 1” is an accept state because now we know our string begins with 0 followed by 1. We’ll also need a null or trap state. This is a state that you enter and you can never reject. Strings that enter this state are doomed to be rejected. Pause and we’ll try to sort this one out in the empty diagram below.











Figure 2.3: What transitions are needed to complete this diagram for strings starting in 01?



Figure 2.3 should have two arrows going to the trap state. We note that every state has a transition “out” on both a 0 and a 1. This is what makes our machine deterministic (more on that later). You’ll also notice that once we are “happy” with our answer, we have states that loop to themselves on all inputs. These are states that have no other transitions out of them and thus, “eat” the rest of input until accept or reject can be determined. This may seem a little silly, and indeed is part of the motivation for RFAs in the next chapter. Take a look and compare your solution by selecting the reveal below.


The Solution Revealed - M3












Figure 2.4: The language of this machine is the set of all strings that start with “01”.




Another common pattern are strings that “end” in a sequence. Let’s focus on strings that end in “01”. This DFA will need only 3 states. There is no trap state because, we keep processing the string until we get to the end. Only when we are at the end do we know what the last two characters should have been. A blank template is below for us to try our a solution.











Figure 2.5: What transitions are needed to complete this diagram for strings that end in 01?





The Solution Revealed - M4












Figure 2.6: The language of this machine is the set of all strings that end in “01”.




Next up are strings that contain certain symbols. Continuing our example, we may look for strings that contain “01”. These strings can begin with any symbol and end in any symbol. You can attack this using Figure 2.5! This means it also only needs three states. Once you’ve “seen” 01, you can accept, so some of the transitions change ever so slightly. See the results in Figure 2.7 below!











Figure 2.7: The language of this machine is the set of all strings that contain “01” anywhere in the string.




We’ve now seen four trends in DFAs that are quite common. Strings that do modular counting, like Figure 2.2, strings that start with a sequence like Figure 2.4, strings that end with a sequence like Figure 2.6, and strings that contain a sequence like Figure 2.7. Turns out DFAs can do even more, but let’s practice these latest pieces.

Create a machine that ends with 111.
Create a machine that contains 010.
Create a machine that start with a 1 AND end with a 0.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.4 Modular Arithmetic
This section requires a moderate level of comfort with binary numbers and the modulus operator, but we build some of the key components and reminders in this section. With the limited memory of a DFA, it is quite surprising that DFAs can perform modular arithmetic. When thinking of a number as a binary number, adding a 0 to the end of a number is the same as multiplying it by 2. In decimal “3” becomes “30” when we add the 0. In binary “10”, or 2, becomes “100”, or 4, when we add a 0. When adding a 1 we’re multiplying by 2 and then adding 1 in binary. Thus “100” or 4, becomes “1001” or 9. In decimal, adding a 1 is multipying by 10 and adding 1; 30 becomes 301 = 30*10 + 1. In turns out, that multiplications and additions to a number also apply to numbers classification in modulus. Remember, modulus is like the remainder after long division - and in programming we generally use % to represent the modular operator. Thus 4%3 and 1%3 are both 1, 2%3 and 5%3 are 2, 3%3 and 6%3 are 0. Let’s look at 1010, or 10 in decimal. 10 should be 1%3. Before looking at the number, we’re in 0%3. When we look at the first 1, we’re now in 1 because 1%3 is 1. Taking in the next 0 multiplies the number by 2 (the number 2 now) and the same with modulus, so we’re in 2%3. The next 1 is times 2 plus 1, so the number is now 5 (2*2+1), and the modulus is 2%3 (because 5%3 is 2). Now the final 0 makes our number,5*2=10, and it does the same to our modulus (times 2). 2*2=4 and 4%3 = 1. Thus, by processing each symbol, we can track the modulus and “end” in the final modulus. Figure 2.8: This machine computes the input mod 3; it accepts strings representing binary numbers divisible by 3.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.5 Determinism
In this chapter, we have been assuming that our machines are deterministic finite automata. A machine is deterministic, if we can trace the path through the machine with a single finger and we never fall off. If a machine is defined formally with a set of states, \(Q\) and an input alphabet, \(A\), then \(Q \times A\) is the cartesian product of those two sets. This means that given an element of \(Q \times A\) it can be listed as \((q,a)\) where \(q\) is an element of Q (a state) and \(a\) is an element of \(A\) an input symbol. A machine is deterministic if for every element of \(Q \times A\) there is a single result in the transition table that is also an element of \(Q\). Writing this fully mathematically, we might say \(Q \times A \rightarrow Q\). To put this in terms of developers (especially typed), the transition table is a function that returns a Q given a Q and an A. In code you might write the signature as:
Q f(Q,A);
Given any Q and an A, we always know exactly which Q we’ll get to. That’s deterministic. There is no guess work, no branching, we run the function and go where it tells us. Taking a look at Figure 2.2, we have built a transition table below.

Figure 2.9: Transition Table of Figure 2.2



Notice that every cell in this table has a single value. f(A,0) returns \(B\). f(B,1) returns \(B\) also. We start in the start state and every transition “deterministically” tells us where to go next. Determinism is great in the sense that we can directly look up where we should go next in a table like this. It is useful in processing with a machine and also in proofs! Sometimes it can be harder for humans to create these machines and thus several of the following chapters discuss variants of these machines to enable easier human processing or proof techniques. Something could be nondeterministic if it could end up in more than one state, fall off the machine, or freely jump around the machine without eating input. We’ll tackle nondeterminism in future chapters.

title: 3  Finite Automata For Developers (RFAs)
text:
3.1 Ramsey’s Finite Automata (RFAs)
This chapter discusses strategies for understanding and working with Ramsey’s Finite Automata (RFAs) with null transitions and halt states. We will cover the basics of RFAs, including their definition, how to construct them, and how to use them to recognize languages. Some approaches are slightly unique, but it is designed to help developers understand the material in a way that is intuitive and practical, especially for programmers or thinking about these problems in a programmatic way. We will be using examples and exercises to help practice and solidify our understanding of RFAs. By the end of this chapter, we should have a good grasp of what RFAs are, how they are slightly different from DFAs, and how to use them effectively.
We introduce an additional kind of state. It is a special accept state that also halts the machine, the halt and accept state denoted as ha or acc with a double circle. Machines can have a halt and reject state, *hr** as well, sometimes synonmous with a null or trap state depending on the type of finite machine we’re using. If the machine ever enters the halt and accept state, it halts and accepts the input string as being in the language of the machine. We’ll add some additional power to the Ramsey Finite Automata (RFAs) presented in this book to align with our notions as programmers as well, but first, let’s give some background on why we use the notation that we do.
In a programming language like C, strings are arrays of characters that are terminated by the null character. In C++ this is represented as ‘\0’. In an ASCII table, this is character 0 - often considered a non-printable character although NUL may be seen if you try to print it out in some situations. The character ‘0’ is number 48 on the ASCII table. In any case, a string like “hello” is actually stored as an array of 6 characters. One character for ‘h’, ‘e’, ‘l’, ‘l’, and ‘o’ and then one more for the terminating character – the null character or \0. We’ll denote detecting the end of a string (and later the end of other things) by using the null character. This means that we’ll see \0 on some of our transitions to denote that we’ve detected the end of a string. Typically this is non-traditional and finite automata run until they eat all the input symbols, but we find this can be a helpful tool when thinking about these machines as developers. Some examples of this expression will be explored below.
The end of string (EOS) character is the null character \0.

title: 3  Finite Automata For Developers (RFAs)
section: 3.2 Traditional Finite Automata vs Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA)
text:
3.2 Traditional Finite Automata vs Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA)
Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs) and RFAs differ because RFAs add halt states and null transitions. As shown in the stoplight example Figure 2.1, in the real world, many FA will operate continuously. DFAs can have many accept states but RFAs should have one (ha). When a DFA finishes processing an input string, it will accept if it is in an accept state (state with a double circle), otherwise it will reject the input string. In an RFA, processing stops when ha is touched. RFAs are not more powerful, but they operate more closely to how we would write simple pattern recognizers in our own code. In addition, these additional operators work similarly to machines we’ll look at in the future. As motivation for RFAs, imagine a language that only needs to look at the first symbol of an input string; strings that begin with an a only require looking at that first character. Such a machine could immediately halt and accept or halt and reject based on that very first symbol and that is exactly the code you’d write. So, an RFA can model the code you’d write by immediately taking a halt-and-accept state to end processing after viewing the first letter.
Converting between the formats is not difficult but it can require some elements of nondeterminism that we’ll see in a future chapter. To turn a traditional DFA into an RFA follow two simple steps. Add a transition from each of those former accept states to a new halt and accept state on a \0 transition. Then turn every accept state from the DFA into a normal state. Other optimizations might exist, but this is a full conversion from DFA to RFA. Converting from an RFA to a traditional FA is a bit more complicated as we must take special care to end in an accept state which does not halt. We’ll use some elements from the nondeterministic chapter to make this transition. Ultimately, we can replace \0 transitions with ~ transitions. The main point is that the two models are not that different and we can convert between them with a little bit of work. The RFA model is more convenient for some purposes but the traditional DFA model can be useful in other areas. Different FA models appear in different places as more powerful tools in certain situations and to give access to different proof techniques (we’ll see four total in this book). Using the right tools for the job is part of the process of becoming a good computer scientist.
